episodes.201755: A few transient supercell type thunderstorms affected portions of eastern West Virginia and the central Virginia Piedmont.
episodes.201760: A weak area of low pressure interacted with an anomalously moist airmass and stalled frontal boundary. This spawned showers and thunderstorms that resulted in localized amounts of one to five inches of rain. The higher amounts were where storms trained or stalled.
episodes.201769: Intense daytime heating combined with a westward moving outflow boundary from a storm complex in Texas resulted in the development of strong to severe storms across the east slopes of the Sacramento Mountains during the early afternoon hours. These storms moved northeast across east central and southeast NM during the afternoon and evening hours bringing strong outflow wind gusts of up to 67 mph at the Roswell Air Center, large hail to trained spotters in western De Baca and northeast Roosevelt County, and a 70 mph wind gust to the mesonet station at Melrose Range. Additionally, nearby thunderstorms brought a 68 mph wind gust to Raton Crews Airport. Storms exited into West Texas just after sunset.||Key Words: Severe Thunderstorm Winds, Large Hail.
episodes.201772: Several trough axes extending southward into northern Alabama and southern middle Tennessee from a stalled frontal boundary extending through the Ohio Valley into the Mid-Atlantic area. These trough axes interacted with an unstable atmopshere to produce a number of strong lines of thundestorms that moved from west to east across northern Alabama. Some of these storms produced damaging winds up to 60 mph.
episodes.201807: A mid-level trough over the Mississippi River, along with subtropical ridging over the northern Gulf and eastward into the Atlantic, brought fairly moist southwesterly flow to Central Alabama. Afternoon convection resulted in a few strong to severe storms, with areas of tree damage in Cherokee, Jefferson, Tallapoosa, and Chambers counties. Later that evening, slow-moving thunderstorms dropped a few inches of rain over southern Lamar County, with several roadways being flooded or washed out.
episodes.201874: A tropical like airmass allow for thunderstorms to produce very heavy rainfall across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of June 15th. Several roads were closed due to flooding.
episodes.201981: The middle of the month featured a front stalled across Ohio, southern Pennsylvania, and northern West Virginia while an upper trough and low pressure system pivoted overhead. Showers and storms began to develop in the moist and unstable environment by the night of June 13th. A lull in precipitation occurred on the morning of the 14th, then activity redeveloped and persisted through the next couple of days as the front meandered across the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians. The front finally began to lift north as a warm front and pulled away from the area on the 17th.||Storms during this time were very efficient rainfall producers, evidenced by two rainfall reports from around the area which noted nearly an inch and a quarter of rain falling within the space of thirty minutes. A few other locations reported daily rainfall amounts in excess of three inches. In addition to rapid rainfall accumulations, multiple rounds of rain over several days helped to saturate the ground and led to one instance of localized flooding in Carter County.
episodes.201982: A multi-day period of flooding occurred in southeast Ohio during the middle of the month due to a stalled front across Ohio, southern Pennsylvania, and northern West Virginia while an upper level disturbance pivoted overhead. Showers and storms began to develop in the moist and unstable environment by the night of June 13th. A lull in precipitation occurred on the morning of the 14th, then activity redeveloped and persisted through the next couple of days as the front meandered across the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians. The front finally began to lift north as a warm front and pulled away from the area on the 17th.||Storms during this time were very efficient rainfall producers, evidenced nearby rainfall reports which noted nearly an inch and a quarter of rain falling within the space of a thirty minutes. A few other locations reported daily rainfall amounts in excess of three inches. In addition to rapid rainfall accumulations, these episodic rounds of heavy rain helped to saturate the ground and led to flash flooding on several roads within southeast Ohio.
episodes.201983: The middle of the month proved to be active across the state of West Virginia in response to a stalled frontal boundary across Ohio, southern Pennsylvania, and northern West Virginia while an upper level disturbance pivoted overhead. Showers and storms began to develop in the moist and unstable environment by the night of June 13th. A lull in precipitation occurred the morning of the 14th, then activity redeveloped and persisted through the next couple of days as the front meandered across the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians. The front finally began to lift north as a warm front and pulled away from the area on the 17th.||Storms during this time were very efficient rainfall producers, evidenced by two rainfall reports from West Virginia which noted nearly an inch and a quarter of rain falling within the space of thirty minutes. A few other locations reported daily rainfall amounts in excess of three inches. In addition to rapid rainfall accumulations, multiple rounds of rain over several days helped to saturate the ground and led to flash flooding across portions of the area. Excess runoff also led to rises on smaller creeks and streams.||Flash flooding impacted several counties including Calhoun, Doddridge, Harrison, Jackson, Kanawha, Pocahontas, Ritchie, Upshur, Webster, and Wood. In addition to numerous flooded roadways across the area, a mudslide occurred in Doddridge County, water rescues were needed in Webster County due to windshield high floodwaters, and one Jackson County road was rendered impassable from logs and other debris deposited by floodwaters.||In addition to the high water observations from storms during this event period, storms grew strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts on the afternoon of June 13th. The combination of strong June solar heating and the nearby frontal boundary resulted in storms to form across the western portions of the state during the peak of the afternoon and tracked eastward as the evening progressed. This produced a swath of of tree and power line damage from Wayne County and northeastward through Upshur County in the midst of the adverse weather. Since storms were primarily diurnally driven, activity quickly waned after sunset on the evening of the 13th.
episodes.202029: Scattered thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall during the evening hours.
episodes.202220: Thunderstorms brought strong winds to southeast Weld and Morgan Counties during the evening of June 14th with gusts as high as 73 mph.
episodes.202283: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms caused localized flooding across portions of Virginia during the afternoon and evening of June 15, 2025. These showers and thunderstorms were in association with a vigorous upper level shortwave trough and quasi-stationary boundary meandering over the area. A general two to four inches of rain fell across areas where flooding occurred.
episodes.202286: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms caused localized flooding across portions of Maryland during the afternoon and evening of June 15, 2025. These showers and thunderstorms were in association with a vigorous upper level shortwave trough and quasi-stationary boundary meandering over the area. A general two to four inches of rain fell across areas where flooding occurred.
episodes.202368: The typical severe weather setup across the region - surface moisture advected in from the east with stronger west to southwesterly flow aloft - developed across the region from June 13-15. Fog and low clouds inhibited destabilization on June 13. Initially surface moisture was less quality on June 14, but increased for June 15, which was the most active severe day.
episodes.202653: A line of thunderstorms developed in southwestern Kansas and moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle and the northern and eastern Texas Panhandle. Wind gusts up to 66 mph occurred with this line of thunderstorms.
episodes.202743: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorm activity impacted portions of Oklahoma, mainly central and northern areas, from the morning of the 14th through daybreak on the 15th. An initial decaying complex of thunderstorms moved from southern Kansas into northern and central Oklahoma on the morning into early afternoon of the 14th. While this activity was non-severe for much of its journey across the WFO Norman Forecast Area, a brief uptick in intensity occurred after midday across southeastern Oklahoma, where sporadic damaging wind gusts and large hail were noted. ||While a brief lull in convective coverage occurred through the early evening, a warming airmass near remnant thunderstorm outflow across west-central Oklahoma provided focus for the development of a lone intense supercell thunderstorm. This thunderstorm impacted portions of Custer, Blaine, Caddo and Washita Counties, producing a tornado and large to very large hail. As a broader synoptic trough impinged across the region later in the evening, more widespread coverage of severe thunderstorms occurred, yielding continued large hail and thunderstorm wind damage events across central and southern Oklahoma through daybreak on the 15th.
episodes.202744: As a broad synoptic trough impinged across the Southern Plains early on the morning of the 15th, widespread thunderstorm development occurred. A semi-organized line of thunderstorms produced observations of severe wind gusts across western-north Texas near and shortly after daybreak.
episodes.202836: Strong storms would move into north central South Dakota during the early morning hours of June 15th. A trained spotter in Glencross would observe 1 inch hail while the Grand River Remote Automatic Weather Station would record a peak wind gust of 62 mph.
episodes.202867: Severe thunderstorms impacted the southern Nebraska panhandle the evening of June 15th. The primary impact was strong winds.
episodes.202924: On the evening of June 14, 2025, isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed along a warm front positioned across northeast Nebraska. Due to weak shear and limited forcing for ascent, most storms quickly intensified before rapidly collapsing. One storm in particular produced a report of 1 hail approximately 5 miles west-southwest of Crofton, NE. Thunderstorm activity gradually diminished through the overnight hours.
episodes.203320: A trough of low pressure over the southern Appalachians combined with a southward moving backdoor cold front in Virginia for the development of scattered to numerous showers and storms over the northern Piedmont and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina in the evening hours. Trees were down due to strong storms in Nash and Halifax, as well as isolated flooding in Johnston County.
episodes.203347: Thunderstorms produced strong winds over the waters.
episodes.203794: A weak shortwave trough rounding an upper-level ridge and upslope flow resulted in scattered thunderstorms over the mountains. A few of these thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts.
episodes.203848: Southwest steering flow over a moist and unstable airmass triggered scattered strong storms as the sea breezes moved inland.
episodes.203849: Southwest steering flow over a moist and unstable airmass triggered scattered strong storms as the sea breezes moved inland.
episodes.203900: Scattered storms developed across central and southeast Virginia during the afternoon and evening of June 15. These storms were slow-moving and produced locally heavy rain and flooding.
episodes.203903: A stationary front was located across central Virginia on June 15. This front slowly moved southwest through the afternoon. Widespread storms developed during the afternoon and continued into the evening on June 15. Some of these storms became severe and produced damaging winds and isolated hail across central Virginia.
episodes.203904: A stationary front was located across central Virginia to northeast North Carolina on June 15. This front slowly moved southwest through the afternoon. Widespread storms developed during the afternoon and continued into the evening on June 15. These storms produced locally heavy rain and flash flooding across portions of central and southeast Virginia. Additionally, an isolated storm produced flash flooding across portions of north-central Virginia in the early morning hours of June 15 after midnight.
episodes.203905: A stationary front was located across central Virginia to northeast North Carolina on June 15. This front slowly moved southwest through the afternoon. Widespread storms developed during the afternoon and continued into the evening on June 15. These storms produced locally heavy rain and flash flooding across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.204009: Disorganized clusters of afternoon summertime thunderstorms developed at peak heat in across portions of north and central Georgia. Modest cold pool formation allowed a few storms to develop strong to damaging winds. Damage was scattered.
episodes.204125: Severe thunderstorms produced strong to severe winds across portions of the Big Country south into portions of the Concho Valley and the Heartland.
episodes.204150: A waterspout was reported by a pilot offshore from Stuart.
episodes.204176: Numerous showers and thunderstorms impacted parts of the Ark-La-Tex region during the afternoon and early evening hours on June 14th as convection continued to develop and locally expand in coverage as a result of colliding outflow boundaries. Much of the region remained quite moist and unstable in advance of the developing convection, with MLCAPE values as high as 2000 to 3000 J/kg and precipitable water values near 2 inches. One of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across northern Caddo Parish where multiple trees were downed near Black Bayou Lake in Hosston.
episodes.204188: Wind gusts up to 59 MPH were reported in Yuma County with a group of thunderstorms moving southeast.
episodes.204282: Westerly flow with embedded disturbances was in place over the area, which allowed for strong to severe thunderstorms to develop along the Rampart Mountains and push across El Paso County through the late afternoon and early evening.
episodes.204405: A stalled frontal boundary located in southern Virginia interacted with a very unstable environment to produce severe thunderstorms in south-central Virginia. The thunderstorm winds from these storms caused tree and power line damage.  Moisture was abundant across the area, with precipitable water values observed at between 1.7 and 1.9 inches.  Storms were progressive however, and observed moving to the east at 15 to 20 mph, which did not allow them to remain situated over any single location for long.
episodes.204409: A severe thunderstorm resulted in a wind gust of 63 mph that caused a downed power pole. The thunderstorm produced a outflow that picked up dust causing a decrease in visibilities to less than a quarter mile in Cochise County.
episodes.204535: A moist and moderately unstable environment in wake of a departing mid-level shortwave supported afternoon thunderstorms.
episodes.204697: Pulse-type showers and thunderstorms continued during the afternoon hours with torrential rainfall rates. Due to a lack of shear, slow moving/nearly stationary storm motion heightened flash flooding threats, particularly over urban areas. A storm developed over Tupelo, MS and dumped buckets of rain over the area resulting in widespread flash flooding. The airport recorded 3.43 inches and set a daily rainfall record.
episodes.204730: A thunderstorm developed in the lee of the Bighorn Range and became severe as it crossed interstate 25 south of Buffalo. A rancher reported half dollar size hail with the storm.
episodes.204749: River flooding was observed along the Black and Fourche LaFave Rivers.
episodes.204840: On the evening of June 14th, a slow moving thunderstorm passed over portions of Ohio County just east of the city of Wheeling. It's slow movement and interaction with another storm allowed for very heavy rainfall in a short period of time. In addition, precipitable water values were very high - in the 90th percentile. A local IFLOWS gage near Valley Grove recorded over 3 inches in an hour. This resulted in catastrophic flash flooding in Little Wheeling Creek and its tributaries. This impacted the towns of Valley Grove, Triadelphia, Elm Grove, and Woodsdale. Nine people were killed, at least 70 cars were pulled out of the creeks, 37 properties were completely destroyed, and another 700 properties had damage ranging from minimal to major. Damage estimates for road damage were 3.5 million. A presidential disaster declaration was issued in late July.
episodes.204921: A typical summertime regime of high atmospheric moisture content and generally low shear was in place across the region. One storm in the Mississippi Sound produced a waterspout as it moved along a stalled microscale boundary that was stalled in the area.
episodes.204954: Following the catastrophic flooding that occurred in portions of Wheeling, WV late on the 14th, another round of slow moving storms developed along a stationary boundary over portions of northern West Virginia. With climatologically high precipitable water values, rainfall was efficient, allowing for 2-4 inch/hr rates. This impacted several counties in northern West Virginia but the hardest hit was the city of Fairmont, where up to 4 inches of rain fell in an hour over the city and surrounding suburbs. Several water rescues were performed and structures were damaged. As of the last count, 22 homes were destroyed and another 283 homes had damage ranged from minor to major just in Marion county alone.
episodes.204956: Weak warm advection initiated isolated convection in a low-shear, high CAPE environment. Slow moving storms made the most of strong initial updrafts to produce hail up to half-dollar size, followed by damaging wind gusts later in storm evolution.
episodes.204957: Weak warm advection initiated isolated convection in a low-shear, high CAPE environment. Slow moving storms made the most of strong initial updrafts to produce hail up to half-dollar size, followed by damaging wind gusts later in storm evolution.
episodes.205009: Ample moisture and a near-stationary boundary assisted in the development of slow moving thunderstorms late on June 14th. Precipitable water values exceeding 90% of climatology, which supported efficient rainfall. Catastrophic flash flooding occurred in portions of Wheeling WV and that complex of storms expanded eastward, dumping 2-3 inches in an hour over portions of Washington county as well. There were several reports of stranded vehicles and flooding around an into some homes.
episodes.205013: Stationary boundary and near climatological max precpitable water led to another round of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall on the 15th. With weak steering flow, storms were allowed to train over one another, producing rainfall amounts in the 2-4 inches range in as little as an hour.
episodes.205018: During the second and third weeks of June 2025, the North Slope of Alaska experienced significant flooding as a result of rapid snowmelt. The region underwent one of its latest seasonal breakups on record, driven by persistently below-average to record-low temperatures throughout May and into early June, accompanied by continued snowfall through the first week of June. This prolonged cold period was followed by an abrupt transition to well above-average to record-high temperatures, which triggered rapid snowmelt and flooding between June 12 and 16.
episodes.205021: Stationary boundary and near climatological max precpitable water led to another round of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall on the 15th. With weak steering flow, storms were allowed to train over one another, producing rainfall amounts in the 2-4 inches range in as little as an hour.
episodes.205159: A stationary front across the Mid-West portion of the CONUS led to a ample warm sector with plenty of moisture and warm air streaming into the Natural State which led to multiple days of severe weather which included tornadoes, wind damage, and several instances of flash flooding across the state as Arkansas saw several days of moderate to heavy rainfall.
episodes.207180: Showers and storms moved across eastern Kentucky as a stalled stationary front sat near the Ohio River and northern Kentucky through the day, putting much of the state in the warm and unstable sector. A digging 500mb trough also pushed east into the Ohio Valley during the day and points southwest, leading to height falls and enhanced lift over eastern Kentucky. Storms had impacted eastern Kentucky for several days, including this particular day, leading to flooding. In fact, a trained spotter in McCreary County reported a 24 hour rain total of 1.99 inches and a 72 hour total of 4.89 inches.
episodes.207321: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms formed ahead of a stationary front extending from Paducah, KY to Greenwood, IN, to Columbus OH.  Storms south of this line were fairly benign in nature however one had enough low level wind sheer to produce a funnel cloud in Wayne county.
